ideas.name: shoulder gravity-compensation spring
ideas.description: A printed bracket on the base and a printed anchor on the upper arm hold an extension spring (or a stack of 2-3 springs) across the shoulder-lift joint, offset from the axis so its moment roughly follows the arm's cos(theta) gravity moment. It offsets about 0.3-0.4 N*m of the 0.41 N*m the arm needs to hold itself, which frees servo torque for payload (0.15 N*m per 100 g). Elbow and wrist servos are unchanged.
needs: extension spring set, about 1 N/mm, 40 mm free length (new item, est. $6, 3 d)
ideas.test: Model the spring as a joint-space torque on shoulder_lift (k, preload, anchor offset). Re-run tuna_fish_can, pudding_box and mustard_bottle and check that shoulder torque at 30 mm lift stays below about 80% of 1.62 N*m. Check that the held groups' approach poses are not pulled off target by the spring at no load.

ideas.name: long-stroke prismatic jaw
ideas.description: A rack and pinion on two 3x150 mm ground steel rods with a 75 mm/rad pitch-radius pinion slides the moving finger straight along the closing axis over about 103 mm. The face stays parallel and the fingertip stays at the fixed fingertip's height at every opening, so it reaches below the top of 34-58 mm tall objects up to 96 mm wide.
needs: steel_rod_3x150 x2 (new item, est. $2 each, 2 d)
ideas.test: A prismatic jaw builder that allows drive_mm_per_rad up to 75 and rod length 150 mm, tried on the tuna_fish_can, pudding_box, sugar_box and mustard_bottle groups.

ideas.name: crowned (convex-cylinder) moving pad
ideas.description: A printed moving-jaw pad whose face is a convex circular arc of about 35 mm radius in the vertical plane, spanning about ±35 deg and about 30 mm tall, with a 3 mm TPU skin (mu 0.9) and the existing 5 mm V-groove running along it. Against a flat vertical side, contact always happens where the arc's tangent is vertical, so the squeeze stays horizontal at any hinge angle. The jaw's turning only moves the contact up or down the arc. The fixed jaw keeps its flat pad.
ideas.test: Pad geometry option in design/fingers.py: replace the flat tilted moving-pad face with an arc of radius crown_mm (20-60) centred behind the pad. Expose crown_mm and arc span as parameters and generate the contact mesh from the arc.

ideas.name: self-aligning pivoting moving pad
ideas.description: The moving pad is mounted on a horizontal pin through its mid-height, parallel to the jaw hinge, running in two MR63 bearings. A light torsion spring centres it about 20 deg back, and it can rotate ±30 deg. On contact the pad rotates under the contact moment until its face lies flat against the object's side, so the normal is horizontal and opposed to the fixed face at every opening from 17 to 85 mm. This removes the revolute's 6-40 deg face tilt that squeezes boxes and large balls down and out. The fixed pad stays as it is (flat, TPU, grooved).
needs: m3_screw x1 (on hand, as the pivot pin)
small torsion spring about 0.02 N*m/rad (new item, est. $2, 3 d)
ideas.test: The simulator needs a pads variant whose moving-pad face is a hinged body with a joint stiffness (centring angle, stiffness, ±range) on the moving jaw. Run it on gelatin_box (now 26 deg down), apple (27 deg), tennis_ball (16 deg) and the held banana and dice.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=3, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=20, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=0, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out: 19 of the 30 failing tasks show this. The stock moving face turns with its hinge, so the moving jaw pushes the object down at an angle: 15-23 deg on the golf ball, lemon, plum and racquetball, 29-32 deg on the tennis ball, apple and soup can, and 48 deg on the gelatin box. Bare PLA has friction 0.45, which only holds a contact tilted up to atan(0.45) = 24 deg. Round objects also have nothing to centre them.
proposals.principle: A tilted contact squeezes the object out when tan(a) is bigger than mu. Tilting the moving pad back by pad_angle makes it parallel at that opening and cuts the tilt over the 42-75 mm range. A TPU skin (mu 0.9) holds contacts up to 42 deg. A V-groove centres spheres, which friction alone cannot trap.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the cheapest fix. All items are on hand: m2 screws and about 18 machine minutes of PLA+TPU printing, so $0 and no lead time. With a 20 deg pad, the leftover tilt is about 28 deg on the gelatin box (tan 0.53, well under 0.9) and about 10-12 deg on the tennis ball and apple. At 17 mm the pad is about 19 deg off the other way (bottom in). tan(19 deg) = 0.34, still far under 0.9, so small objects stay held. No params move can do this: System 1 already searched every grasp setting, and the face tilt is set by geometry at each width.
risks: large_marker / wood_block_cube / foam_brick: narrow objects now meet a pad tilted about 19 deg bottom-in, which pushes them up. TPU's mu of 0.9 is about 2.6x what that needs, so they should hold.
cup / banana: the groove changes where contact lands on a curved surface. The groove is shallow (3 mm) and the higher friction should make up for it.
proposals.result: KEPT: gained flat_screwdriver, golf_ball, lost none; costs $0.00, 5 machine min

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out (the face turns with the hinge: tilt grows from 7 deg at 25 mm to 44 deg at 75 mm) and the moving fingertip rising (+7 to +11 mm at 59-70 mm openings). A pad angle can only correct the tilt at one opening.
proposals.principle: A rack-and-pinion finger neither turns nor rises as it opens. Its contact stays horizontal and opposite the fixed face at every width, so the contacts are antipodal for every object. Squeeze is torque / pinion radius = 1.62/0.060 = 27 N, a bit above the stock 20 N.
proposals.hypothesis: If the pad-angle fix only works over part of the width range, this removes the tilt at every width. 60 mm/rad over the 1.37 rad servo range gives about 82 mm of travel. That covers every rolling or tilted failure up to the 75 mm apple, but not the 85-96 mm boxes and cans. Cost: 2 lm3uu ($2.40) + 2 steel rods ($3.00) = $5.40, 3 days of lead time, and about 178 machine minutes (32 g PLA + pads). The TPU and groove centre and grip the balls.
risks: cup: if its width is over about 82 mm, the jaw can no longer open wide enough. That would be the one held group to lose.
potted_meat_can: about 57 mm wide, so within travel. The added wrist mass (rods and printed rack) slightly raises the shoulder load, but the can held before with margin.
small held objects: squeeze goes up from 20 to 27 N, which should be harmless on rigid objects.

proposals.edit: jaw -> parallelogram (link_mm=80); pads -> pads (groove_mm=3, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=0, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=0, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out: the moving face's orientation changes with the opening, leaving it 14-44 deg off parallel over 35-75 mm.
proposals.principle: A four-bar carries the finger without turning it, so the face stays vertical and parallel to the fixed face at every opening. Against a sphere, a vertical face touches at the equator however far the fingertip has risen, so the contact pushes neither up nor down. An 80 mm link keeps the lever close to the stock 81 mm, which keeps squeeze at about 20 N and an opening close to the stock 99 mm.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the fallback to the prismatic jaw. It keeps the stock jaw's wide swing, so the cup and any wide held object keep their opening, and it is cheaper: 4 mr63 bearings ($3.60), 3 days, about 100 machine minutes. The fingertip still rises R(1-cos q), but on parallel faces that only moves the contact up the side, not off the antipodal line.
risks: low held objects (foam_brick, wood_block_cube): the fingertip rises with the opening. With the link near the stock radius, the rise should be close to the stock rise those objects already pass with.
the cup and banana touch curved sides through a groove: the groove is only 3 mm deep, and TPU raises friction.

iterations.notes: I didn't propose anything for arm_stall on tuna, pudding and sugar. The only fix in the catalogue is servos_12v, and its parts cost $14 + 3 × $18 = $68 against the $40 budget, so it's out. Also, the reg_ runs of pudding, sugar and mustard fail because the moving jaw lands on the top face: at 0.57-0.63 rad the fingertip is 7-9 mm high and the face is tilted 30 deg or more. Even fixing that, the jaw would have to open to about 0.9-1.1 rad, where the stock hinge tilts 53-64 deg. The rva000_ runs of pudding and sugar stall the arm instead; rva000_mustard is a fixed-jaw miss. So the wide boxes and cans most likely need both a parallel jaw and more arm torque. Buying 12 V servos needs more budget. Proposal 1 is free and should be tried first. Proposals 2 and 3 each cost under $6 if 1 doesn't hold across the width range.

iterations.notes:
I sent three proposals: two pad-angle settings to trial and one untested idea for the arm stalls.

**Main problem.** Most of the remaining failures come from one cause. With the pads at 20°, the moving jaw's face is parallel to the fixed face only at about 0.34 rad, roughly a 33 mm opening. But 11 of the 13 failing objects close at 0.45 to 0.85 rad, where the face tilts outward at the bottom. On those objects the moving jaw pushes the object downward:
- 20° on the tennis ball
- 24° on the soup can
- 27° on the apple
- 33° on the gelatin box
- 7–13° on the balls between 45 and 60 mm

**Proposals 1 and 2: move the parallel point.**
- **Proposal 1** sets the pad angle to 33°. The faces become parallel at about 50 mm, which suits the wider objects best.
- **Proposal 2** is the safer version: 29°, plus a deeper groove (4 mm) and wider pads (18 mm). These target the 45–60 mm balls, which partly touch the bare plastic of the stock jaw above the pad.

Both are free: they use parts on hand and take about 18 and 27 minutes of printing.

**What they put at risk.** The narrow held objects (the marker and screwdriver at about 17–25 mm) would see the face tilt the other way, 19–25° inward at the bottom, which pushes them up. tan 25° is 0.47, well under the pad friction of 0.9, so I expect them to hold. The banana is the other risk, because a parallel-face jaw already lost it once.

**What I expect them not to fix.** The gelatin box also fails because the moving fingertip ends 16 mm above the fixed one. A pad angle can't change that, so its gain is uncertain.

**Proposal 3: arm stalls (idea only).** The arm stalls on the tuna can, pudding box and mustard bottle. The catalogue fix, the 12 V servos, costs $68 against $40 left. Instead I recorded an untested idea: a spring across the shoulder joint that carries most of the arm's own 0.41 N*m. It needs a spring set I estimate at $6 with 3 days' lead time.

**Out of reach this iteration.** The sugar box (92 mm) and mustard bottle (96 mm) are wider than the jaw's 91 mm maximum opening. No catalogue jaw that has kept the held groups gets past that. The dice failure looks like the jaws closing past the object rather than a problem with the jaw faces, so I left it for later.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing two lip trials on the pads and leaving the rest alone for now.

**What the failures are**
- **Round objects:** most failures are squeezed_down_out or slipped_under_load. The cause is the revolute jaw's face tilt: per the brief, about 1 deg per servo degree, from 12 deg in at 17 mm to 42 deg out at 85 mm. That moves the moving contact above the equator.
- **Why I won't fix the tilt directly:** banana fails at every other tilt profile tried (pad_angle 29 and 33, and the parallelogram). The prismatic jaw lost potted_meat_can. My guess is that its tapered sides need the revolute's swung-out face, which a pad_angle on the prismatic jaw cannot give. So I'm adding a catch below the equator (the untried lip_mm) instead.

**The "arm_stall" failures (tuna can, pudding box, mustard)**
- These are not torque failures. Holding the arm takes 0.41 + 0.15 × 1.87 = 0.69 N·m for the 187 g pudding box and about 1.06 N·m for the 431 g mustard. Both are well under the 1.62 N·m stall, and potted_meat_can (370 g) is already held.
- What actually happens is that the load-limit reflex fires when the moving fingertip lands on the top face. It is the same as reg_pudding_box's moving_jaw_on_top_face. At 85 mm the moving fingertip is +28 mm above the fixed one, but the tuna can's top is only about +17 mm.
- So servos_12v would not fix these, and at $68 it is over the $40 budget anyway.

**What nothing in the catalogue fixes**
- Sugar box (92 mm), mustard (96 mm) and pudding box (90 mm) are at or beyond the jaw's 91 mm limit.
- The prismatic jaw tops out at about 82 mm of travel.
- Fixing these needs a wider jaw that doesn't rise as it opens, which is a future idea. I'm not proposing it now, because it would also have to keep the banana's tilt profile.

**Dice**
The dice is squeezed upward by the 12 deg bottom-in tilt at 17 mm. A lip may help a little. I am not predicting a gain.

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out on the gelatin box, tennis ball, apple and tomato soup can. At 65-75 mm the revolute moving face is 23-32 deg off parallel with the bottom swung out, so the moving jaw pushes 20-33 deg down. Also slipped_under_load or never_lifted on the 47-59 mm spheres (moving jaw pushing 4-13 deg down, contacts 3-7 mm above centre), and the dice squirting out at 17 mm (face 12 deg bottom-in, 36 deg up on the fixed side).
proposals.principle: A contact tilted by a pushes the object out with N sin a. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at only one opening. A finger that slides straight neither turns nor rises, so its tilt is whatever the pad gives it, at every width.
proposals.hypothesis: Four pad-parameter trials gained nothing. Every change to pad_angle (29, 33) lost the banana, so no value of the revolute's pad_angle fixes tilt that grows about 1 deg per servo degree. This calls for a jaw redesign. The prismatic jaw was tried once (drive 60, pad_angle 0) and lost only the potted_meat_can to slipped_under_load. That face was exactly vertical, so nothing helped friction carry the 370 g metal can (mu 0.35). This time I give the moving pad a small constant bottom-in tilt of 4 deg. Its upward component, N sin 4 deg (about 1.9 N at 27 N squeeze), helps hold the weight. tan 4 deg = 0.07 is well below every object's friction (0.35-0.9), so nothing is squeezed out. I also use a 3 mm TPU skin and a wider 16 mm pad with a 4 mm groove, for more contact patch and better centring of spheres. Squeeze is 1.62/0.060 = 27 N, more than the revolute's 20 N. Travel is 60 x 1.37 = 82 mm, which covers every target up to the 75 mm apple, and the cup was kept at that travel in iteration 1. Cost: 2 lm3uu ($2.40) + 2 steel rods ($3.00) = $5.40, 3 d lead time, about 160 + 20 machine minutes.
risks: potted_meat_can: lost last time on a vertical prismatic face. The 4 deg bottom-in wedge and the thicker TPU skin are aimed at exactly that slip.

banana: was squeezed up on the parallelogram, which moves the fingertip height. The prismatic jaw does not, and the banana survived the earlier prismatic trial. 4 deg of upward push (tan 0.07) is small.
cup and other wide held objects: travel stays 82 mm, the same as the trial that kept them.

flat_screwdriver and large_marker: thin cylinders could sink deeper into a 5 mm V. That centres them further and does not change tilt.
foam_brick, wood_block_cube, potted_meat_can: flat faces touch the groove edges on a wider pad, so the contact area is unchanged or larger.

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out and slipped_under_load on round and narrow-box objects (tennis_ball, apple, lemon, plum, racquetball, strawberry, tomato_soup_can, gelatin_box). In every one of these the moving face is tilted bottom-out at the closing angle: 33 deg on the gelatin box at 0.88 rad, 25-27 deg on the apple and soup can, 20 deg on the tennis ball, 5-14 deg on the small balls. The moving fingertip also sits +4 to +16 mm above the fixed one, so the moving contact lands above the equator and pushes the object down and out.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at one opening only, and a swinging fingertip rises R(1-cos q). A slide whose finger neither turns nor rises keeps the contacts antipodal and level at every width. The V-groove then centres the sphere instead of fighting a tilt.
proposals.hypothesis: Five pad-only trials show the revolute's tilt can't be fixed by pad_angle. Every pad_angle other than 20 (29 and 33) lost the banana, and lips lost almost everything. So no value in the current part fixes the mechanism, and a jaw swap is justified. The prismatic jaw has been tried twice. With pad_angle 0 (groove 3, width 12, TPU 2) it lost only potted_meat_can, to slipped_under_load, and it kept the banana. With pad_angle 4 it lost the banana (squeezed_up_out), which tells us the banana needs vertical faces, not bottom-in ones. This trial goes back to the pad_angle-0 prismatic but carries the pads that are now held (groove 5, width 20, TPU 3). On revolute those pads gained the dice and lost nothing. The potted-meat slip had a huge linear margin: squeeze 1.62/0.06 = 27 N, 2 x 0.9 x 27 = 49 N against 3.6 N of weight. So it was most likely the long can twisting about the grasp axis. A pad 20 mm wide instead of 12 gives about 1.7x the lever against that twist, and the thicker 3 mm TPU gives a larger contact patch. Travel at 60 mm/rad over 1.37 rad is about 82 mm. That covers every object it targets: the gelatin box at 73 mm, the apple at 75, the soup can at 68, the tennis ball at 66 and the smaller balls. Cost: 2 lm3uu ($2.40) and 2 steel rods ($3.00), so $5.40 and 3 days of lead time. Machine time is 32 g PLA at 5 min/g (160 min) plus about 11 min for the pads, about 171 of the 584 minutes. Screws are on hand.
risks: potted_meat_can: it slipped once on prismatic with 12 mm pads. The wider 20 mm TPU-3 pads are meant to stop the twist, but the trial has to confirm it.
cup: if it is wider than about 80 mm with side clearance, the 82 mm travel may be too short. On revolute it closed within 89 mm.
banana: it held on prismatic with pad_angle 0 before, and the pads here differ only in groove and width, which kept it on revolute.
dice and golf_ball: the slide's squeeze is higher (27 N against 20 N) and the faces don't tilt. That should help these small objects, not hurt them.

For spheres, the contact moves to the ball's equator side of the arc and stops pushing it down. Nothing in the catalogue gives an orientation-independent contact on the hinge, which is why this is recorded as an idea.

idea.name: crowned (convex-cylinder) moving pad
idea.description: A printed moving-jaw pad whose face is a convex circular arc of about 35 mm radius in the vertical plane, spanning about ±35 deg and about 30 mm tall, with a 3 mm TPU skin (mu 0.9) and the existing 5 mm V-groove running along it. Against a flat vertical side, contact always happens where the arc's tangent is vertical, so the squeeze stays horizontal at any hinge angle. The jaw's turning only moves the contact up or down the arc. The fixed jaw keeps its flat pad.
idea.test: Pad geometry option in design/fingers.py: replace the flat tilted moving-pad face with an arc of radius crown_mm (20-60) centred behind the pad. Expose crown_mm and arc span as parameters and generate the contact mesh from the arc.

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out (gelatin box: moving jaw pushing 26 deg down; apple 26-27 deg; tennis ball 15-16 deg) and slipped_under_load on the spheres (moving contact +3 to +4 mm above centre, pushing 4-9 deg down). Both come from the moving face turning with its hinge.
proposals.principle: A contact tilted by a pushes the object down with N sin(a). Once tan(a) gets near mu, the closing servo squeezes the object out. On a sphere, a tilted face touches above the equator and drives the ball downward. A face that keeps its orientation at every opening makes the contacts antipodal at every width, and the V-groove then centres the round objects at the equator.
proposals.hypothesis: The revolute face is parallel at one opening only. The brief puts it 1 deg off at 35 mm, 22 deg at 65 mm and 30 deg at 75 mm. Ten pad-only trials have moved that parallel point around (pad_angle 18 to 33, reach 0 to 30). Each one either gained small objects or lost the banana, cup, dice or potted meat can, so no pad value fixes tilt that grows with opening. The prismatic jaw was tried three times and lost the banana each time. Its 60 mm/rad pinion gives about 27 N of squeeze (1.62/0.06), well above the 20 N every held object was tuned at. The parallelogram has never been tried. With link 80 mm the lever is close to the stock 81 mm, so squeeze stays about 20 N. That protects the potted meat can, which failed with force_limit once the lever grew to about 93 mm, and the banana, which failed under prismatic's harder squeeze. Its face stays vertical at all openings (pad_angle 0, since this jaw doesn't turn), so the 73 mm gelatin box goes from 26 deg to about 0 (cardboard mu 0.5). The apple goes from 27 deg to about 0, and the spheres' moving contacts move from 4 mm above centre to the equator. Fingertip rise is still R(1-cos q), about the same as now at the same link radius, but rise alone is not what fails on these objects: the fixed jaw, which doesn't rise, holds them at the same height. Cost: 4 x mr63_bearing = $3.60 (3 d lead time), 16 g PLA = 80 min, plus the pads, about 12 min.
risks: banana: held at 35 mm where today's face is only 1 deg off, so a vertical face barely changes it, and squeeze stays about 20 N rather than prismatic's 27 N

dice/strawberry/golf_ball (small widths): today the face is 8-14 deg bottom-in at 17-25 mm. Making it vertical changes the up-push they may rely on, and the fingertip height at small openings depends on the four-bar's geometry

proposals.principle: A round object is held at its equator, and a contact above it pushes the object down. reach_mm lengthens the pad past the stock fingertip. With the fingertip still placed with clearance above the table, the pad's upper edge rises by the reach, so the equator contact lands on the tilted, grooved TPU face instead of the edge. A longer radius also closes a given width at a smaller q, which is nearer the parallel point.
proposals.hypothesis: Reach 6 is half of the reach 12 that lost dice and potted_meat_can (force_limit / never_lifted), and a fifth of the reach 25-30 that lost five groups. idea.description: The moving pad is mounted on a horizontal pin through its mid-height, parallel to the jaw hinge, running in two MR63 bearings. iterations.notes:
I'm sending three proposals: two cheap pad-parameter trials and one idea that can't be tested yet.

**Proposal 1: pad_angle 23 → 27, nothing else changed.** It targets the small rolling balls (plum, racquetball, lemon), which slip out during the lift. They close at 42–47 mm, where the moving jaw's face is still tilted 4–9° and presses above the ball's middle, pushing it down. At 27° the face should be parallel at about 42 mm. The safe range is already measured: 25° kept every held group in iteration 7, and 29° lost the banana. 27° is the untested value between them. The banana and dice are the groups at risk.

**Proposal 2: reach 6 mm with pad_angle 25.** On every ball the moving-jaw contact is reported at the top edge of the pad, where it meets the bare stock jaw. That corner sits 3–4 mm above the ball's middle and has half the grip of the TPU pad. Lengthening the pads by 6 mm should move that corner up so the contact lands on the grooved TPU face. Reach 12 lost the dice and potted meat can, so I used half that. It's paired with 25°, the one angle already proven safe. Squeeze falls only from about 20 N to about 18.6 N.

**Proposal 3 (idea): a pivoting moving pad.** For the gelatin box, apple and tennis ball, the moving face is 15–27° off, which pushes them down and out. Ten pad trials only moved the one opening where the face is parallel. All five jaw swaps lost the banana, flat screwdriver or golf ball. A pad on a spring-centred pin would turn to sit flat against the object at any opening while keeping the stock jaw. It needs about $3.80 of parts (two bearings and a small spring).

**Changes I left out:**
- **12 V servos:** about $68, over the $40 budget.
- **Prismatic and parallelogram jaws:** tried five times and always lost held groups, so I didn't repeat them.
- **The wide boxes and the mustard bottle:** they fail because the moving fingertip rises and ends up on the top face. No catalogue part fixes that without the losses above; that's the job of the long-stroke prismatic jaw idea already on record.
- **Tuna can and the second pudding box run:** both "stall" at under 200 g. That should need only about 0.67 N·m against a 1.62 N·m limit, so I suspect the jaw pressing on the top face, not a weak arm. I haven't tested that, and none of these proposals addresses it.

If both pad trials gain groups, iteration 10 could try 27° together with reach 6.

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out (gelatin box, apple) and slipped_under_load (tennis ball): the hinged moving face is 11-26 deg bottom-swung-out at 59-71 mm openings, so its only contact is high on the object (+7 to +23 mm above the centre) and pushes it down.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A round object is pushed up by contacts below its equator and down by contacts above, so one contact above and one below trap it. A tilted contact squeezes the object out unless an opposing contact cancels its vertical push.
proposals.hypothesis: lip_mm is the only pad parameter never changed in 12 pad trials, and it is the only one that adds a contact at the fingertip without moving the parallel point (which pad_angle 29 showed costs the banana) or the lever (which reach 6-30 showed costs the dice, potted meat can, wood block and cup). The reported contact heights put the gap between the bottom of the tilted moving pad and the object at about 4.4 mm for the gelatin box ((12-1) mm x tan 22), 2.9 mm for the apple and 4.2 mm for the tennis ball. A 4 mm lip closes those gaps and adds a second, nearly horizontal contact low on the moving jaw. On the box it acts below the downward-pushing top-edge contact. On the spheres it acts below the equator, so with the upper face it cradles the object vertically. Small held round objects have their fingertips far below the equator (golf ball gap about 8.7 mm, banana about 5 mm), so the lip does not reach them.
risks: dice, wood_block_cube, foam_brick, potted_meat_can: on flat-sided objects the lip strip becomes the first contact at the fingertip, which shrinks the contact patch and may be bare PLA (mu 0.45). The normals stay horizontal, and 2 x 0.45 x 20 N = 18 N still exceeds the potted meat can's 3.6 N weight.
dice: the lips stop the jaw about 4 mm earlier, adding about 3 deg of bottom-in tilt. The dice was lost once to squeezed_up_out.
flat_screwdriver, banana: these are low objects whose lower surface could catch on a lip and be pushed up.
